activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Phishing is a scam in which someone pretends to be a trusted company or person to trick you into giving away passwords or other private information.
story:
The phone sat heavy in Daniel's pocket as he climbed onto the school bus, a rectangle of glass and possibility that his mom had handed over that morning with the words "prove I can trust you." He slid into the seat next to Taylor, who took one look at his face and leaned over. "You finally got it?" Taylor said. "Let me see." Daniel pulled it out carefully, like it might dissolve, and Taylor thumbed through the screens with the ease of a veteran while Daniel watched, half proud and half nervous.

"Text your mom so she knows you got on the bus," Taylor said. "That's the responsible move." Daniel was still typing when the phone buzzed with a message from a number he didn't recognize. The screen read: "ALERT: Your BlockCraft account will be deleted in 24 hours. Verify your password now to keep it." Taylor's older brother had shown him BlockCraft months ago, and Daniel had spent a whole weekend building a castle with a lush garden made of green wool blocks. "Twenty-four hours," he said. "I have to verify. Right now."

Taylor grabbed his wrist. "Wait. My cousin lost fifty dollars like that. Why would the game text you on a random number?" Daniel stared at the message. The spelling of "BlockCraft" was wrong, one letter off, which seemed weird for an official warning. If the game company really wanted to verify him, wouldn't they ask inside the app instead of by text? He thought about what Taylor had said. "They're pretending to be the game," Daniel said slowly. "That has to imply they want something from me."

"Exactly," Taylor said. "It's called phishing. Someone pretends to be a trusted company or person to trick you into giving away your password or private stuff." They looked the word up on Taylor's phone and found a whole page of examples, including texts almost word for word like the one on Daniel's screen. Taylor, who had been begging his own parents for a phone since August and wanted nothing more than to be the guy with answers, sat up straighter. "Told you," he said. "I'm basically security now."

Daniel forwarded the message to his mom, then blocked the number. His thumbs hovered over the reply box, but he closed it without typing anything, because answering at all felt like opening a door. The bus rattled over the speed bump by the gym, and outside, Mr. Santoso was unlocking the doors of the corner store, nodding at the kids through the glass.

"So your first day with a phone," Taylor said, "and you caught a scam before breakfast." Daniel slid the phone back into his pocket and felt its weight there, smaller now. "Text me when you get home," Taylor called over the hiss of the bus brakes. "So I know you didn't get phished." Daniel stepped down onto the curb and grinned. "Verify your password first," he said.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A break statement stops a loop immediately, so a prime checker can quit as soon as it finds a single divisor.
story:
Eli typed 9 into the little black input box and pressed Enter. The program printed "not prime" seven times in a row, stacked like a fence down the screen. He stared at it. He had written the loop himself, checking every number from 2 upward, and somewhere in his logic a single answer had turned into a whole crowd of them.

"Your printer's haunted," said Pierce from the next computer. Pierce wanted the lab period to be over so he could get to the gym before anyone else claimed the good basketball, and he kept glancing at the clock above the whiteboard. "Nine isn't even prime, so at least it's right once."

"But why seven times?" Eli said. He scrolled up through his code, tapping the desk with one finger. The lab smelled like warm dust and the lemon cleaner Mr. Clarke used on the keyboards, and somewhere a fan hummed inside a tower that nobody ever sat at. Eli did not despise debugging exactly, but he was starting to understand people who did. "It finds 3 divides 9, prints not prime, then finds 4 doesn't divide 9, finds 5 doesn't, and prints again for every check that fails."

Frederique leaned over from the far side of him, ponytail swinging, chewing the last of a mint. "So it decides it's not prime, and then it keeps deciding anyway. Like it doesn't trust itself." She taught herself Python from library books and wanted, more than anything on a Thursday, to be the one who saw the fix first. "Don't you want it to just stop?"

Eli sat very still. Stop. The word felt like a key turning. "If it knows the answer the moment it finds one divisor, why is it still looking?" he asked the screen. He scrolled to his textbook, thumbed to the chapter on loops, and ran his finger down the page until he found it: a break statement stops a loop immediately. He read the line twice, then once more, the way you check a door you think you heard click shut.

He typed break into the loop, right after the print, aligned under the if with a tap of the spacebar. His spine straightened as he ran the program again. He entered 9. One clean "not prime," and nothing else. He entered 13, and the machine told him it was prime. He entered 121, just to be sneaky, and got a single "not prime" again. "Pierce," he said, "come look at this before you go."

Pierce dragged himself over, and Frederique squeezed in beside him, and the three of them watched Eli type 2, and the screen said "prime." "Eleven's my number," Pierce said, still half angled toward the gym. "Test eleven."

Eli entered 11.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: In the beep test, or multistage fitness test, runners go back and forth between markers usually 20 meters apart, and the beeps come faster at each new level.
story:
Felix stood at the baseline of the gym with a line of other sixth graders, staring at the orange cones Mr. Paquette had set up. He wanted the basketball team more than he had wanted anything since a remote-control car he'd seen in a commercial made by some corporation that sold toys he couldn't afford. His tryout, though, was not going to be about dribbling. Not yet.

"First we run," said Mr. Paquette, clicking a stopwatch. "We call it the beep test."

Evelyn, next to Felix, groaned. "I hate that thing. It's toxic."

The coach explained only the setup: run to the far cone and back, again and again, and keep up with the beeps from the speaker. Evelyn took off like a startled cat on the first beep, sprinting her out-and-back and getting to the line with seconds to spare. She looked smug. Felix jogged, arriving just before the beep, and she smirked at him too.

But Felix had noticed something. The distance never changed. The cones sat exactly 20 meters apart, so every single leg was the same, out and back, out and back. Nothing about the running itself got harder. What changed was the sound. After a while the speaker gave a double chime, and the next beeps came faster. Then another chime, and faster still. Each new level squeezed the time down, and Evelyn, who was still sprinting to the line early and standing there waiting, was burning everything she had. That was the hidden part, he realized. The test didn't punish you for being slow right now. It punished you for spending too much too soon. It was like the kid in the lunch line who buys three cookies on Monday and has nothing left by Wednesday.

So Felix tested his idea. He stopped trying to arrive early. He timed each leg so he landed on the line just as the beep sounded, no earlier, saving the spare seconds in his legs like coins in a jar. When the beeps sped up, he sped up. Evelyn was still ahead of him at level four, grinning, but her grin was getting thinner.

At level six the chime sounded and the beeps came quicker than ever. Evelyn's sprint left her two steps short of the line, and the second beep caught her standing still, gasping like a fish. "No way," she wheezed, and dropped out beside Makenna, who had quit two levels earlier and was summarizing the injustice of it all to anyone who would listen.

Felix kept going, out to the cone and back, his lungs burning, hitting the line on the beep again and again until his legs finally gave out one stride short at level eight. He lay flat on the gym floor, staring at the ceiling.

Mr. Paquette walked over and looked down at his clipboard. "Nice pacing, kid. See you at practice Monday."

From somewhere above him, Felix heard Evelyn mutter, "I'm learning to jog."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: SUM skips cells that hold text, so a number stored as text is silently left out of the total.
story:
Nathan sat cross-legged on Cameron's bedroom floor with the laptop balanced on a stack of comic books. Their science teacher wanted every group to track plant growth for six weeks, and Cameron's idea was to do it properly: a spreadsheet with a column for each day's measurement, a formula that added the column, and a bar chart to show the whole thing at once.

"You type the numbers," Cameron said, scrolling through a website about bean plants. "I'll read them out."

Nathan built the sheet one row at a time. He typed day labels down the left side, then measurements beside them, and at the bottom of the column he put the formula Cameron's older brother had shown them once: =SUM(B2:B8). He pressed Enter and watched the total appear. Then he clicked the chart button and dragged over the numbers, and seven bars rose up on the screen, one tall and proud, three in the middle, and two that looked oddly flat.

"Wait," Nathan said, leaning closer. "That bar should be bigger. Day four was eleven millimetres, and the chart shows almost nothing." He counted the bars twice, then counted the rows. Seven rows, seven bars. So the chart wasn't missing a day; it was drawing one of them wrong. Or, he wondered, was the drawing right and the total wrong? He checked the SUM at the bottom. It said 41, but when he added the numbers in his head he got 52. He added again on his fingers, slower, and got 52 again.

He clicked on the cell for day four. The eleven was sitting there plain as anything. But when he clicked on a different cell, the one for day two, he noticed something odd in the corner of the screen. Day four's cell had a tiny green triangle in its corner, and day two's didn't. He clicked day four again and saw the number was hugging the left side of the cell, while every other number sat on the right.

"Did you paste this one?" Nathan asked.

Cameron leaned over. "Yeah, from the website. The rest I typed. Why, does it matter?"

Nathan didn't answer right away. He clicked into the cell, deleted the eleven, and typed 11 fresh. The green triangle vanished, the number slid over to the right, the total jumped from 41 to 52, and the fourth bar in the chart shot upward like it had been waiting for permission. So that was it. SUM skips cells that hold text, so a number stored as text is silently left out of the total. The eleven had looked like a number to him, but the formula could tell the difference even though he couldn't, at least not until he noticed which side of the cell it sat on.

"You found it," Cameron said, peering at the screen. "How?"

"Text hugs left, numbers hug right," Nathan said, and clicked the chart again just to watch the tall bar grow.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In a 1950 study of a student housing complex at MIT, Leon Festinger and colleagues found residents most often became friends with the people who lived closest to them.
story:
The moving truck rattled over a pothole, and the box marked DESK STUFF slid until it bumped Hunter's sneaker. He was sitting on the floor between his bike and a lamp shaped like a rocket, because the two men his dad had hired had said he could ride in the back as long as he stayed away from the door. That was fine with him. In the front seat, up with the driver, his dad was probably talking about mortgage rates. Hunter preferred the boxes.

He pulled his notebook out of the desk box and flipped to the page where he'd written his plan. Item one: make friends fast. Item two was blank, which was the problem. At his old school it had taken him most of fourth grade to find Zoey and Hanna, and they'd found him, really, by arguing over whose fault it was that a dodgeball had smashed the library window. He had no idea how to make that happen again on purpose. New town, new street, nobody.

The truck slowed for a toll booth, and Hunter scrutinized his plan the way Mr. Carvalho, his old science teacher, had taught him to scrutinize a hypothesis. Look for evidence. He thought about Zoey and Hanna again and realized something odd: they had lived three doors down from him the whole time. His friend from before that, a boy who'd moved away in third grade, had lived directly across the hall in their old apartment building. Hunter grabbed his pencil and wrote: every friend I've ever had lived super close to me. Coincidence? He chewed the eraser. It seemed like the kind of thing somebody might have actually studied, with real data, and when they got to the new house he would need to find out.

He tested the idea the same afternoon. Their new house was the middle one on a street of five, and Hunter noticed that the moving truck had parked directly between the house on the left and the house on the right. Instead of hauling boxes, he dragged his bike off the truck and rode one slow lap, checking porches. A girl about his age was sitting on the porch of the house on the right, closest to his, untangling a jump rope. He rode past twice before he stopped.

"You're the new kid," she said. Not a question.

"I'm Hunter. I live there." He pointed at the middle house, then at hers. "Basically across the driveway from you."

"Basically," she said. "I'm Hanna, with two Ns in the middle. Want to see if the ice cream truck comes at four?"

They sat on her steps waiting for it, and Hunter told her his hypothesis. She listened all the way through, which he appreciated, because Zoey would have interrupted at least twice.

"So you think closeness picks your friends?" Hanna said. "Actually, that checks out. My dad told me about a study once. In 1950, some researchers studied a student housing complex at MIT, Leon Festinger and some other people, and they found residents most often became friends with the people who lived closest to them."

Hunter sat up straight. "That's my whole notebook page."

"Then your notebook page has famous company," Hanna said, and stood, because the ice cream truck was turning the corner. "Race you. Loser buys."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: A ball rolling on a flat floor gradually slows down because friction and rolling resistance take away its energy.
story:
Alexis crouched at the top of the skate park bowl with a stopwatch in one hand and a tennis ball in the other. Her science homework said to measure the speed of a rolling ball, record the distance it covered every second, and plot the numbers on a distance-time graph. She had tried it in her bedroom the night before, and the graph had come out a jagged mess that made no sense at all.

"Ready?" Jon called from the flat concrete at the bottom, holding a clipboard. Mary stood halfway along with chalk, ready to mark where the ball was at each second. "On three. One, two, three."

Alexis let go. The ball rattled down the slope, shot across the smooth concrete, and rolled, and rolled, and rolled, until Jon had to intervene with his foot to keep it from dropping into the far drain. They measured the chalk marks. Between the first second and the second, the ball had covered almost two meters. Between the fourth and fifth, barely half a meter.

"That can't be right," Alexis said, staring at her notes. "I pushed it exactly the same way as last night."

"It's the ground," Mary said slowly, looking from the concrete to the rubber safety matting that bordered the ramps. "My carpet at home eats my brother's marbles. They just stop."

Alexis remembered then. Her bedroom floor was carpet, thick and soft, and the ball had always quit on her almost immediately. Down here the surface was hard and smooth, so the ball kept going. Something invisible was taking the ball's energy on the way, and it took more on her carpet and less here. She did not know exactly how, but the pattern was clear, and it made her messy data suddenly coherent.

"Let's test it," she said. She rolled the ball twice more on the concrete, then twice across the rubber mat, calling out the seconds while Mary chalked and Jon wrote. The mat runs died in three or four seconds every time. The concrete runs stretched out long and slow, the ball creeping along at the end like a tired jogger. On flat ground, with nothing pushing it, the ball always slowed and always stopped, sooner on the rough surface, later on the smooth one.

She sat on the edge of the bowl and drew two graphs side by side. The concrete curve bent gently, flattening out. The mat curve practically fell over. Then she checked the inflation of the tennis ball, squeezing it, and found it soft and squishy, which probably had not helped either. She had one more idea.

"Jon, run to the dollar store and get a pump needle. Mary, hold the stopwatch."

She set the ball on the chalk line, waiting for it to be firm, ready to roll again.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: A heritage language is one spoken at home or in the family that differs from the main language of the wider community, and heritage speakers may speak it without reading it.
story:
The group chat lit up at 9:14 on a Saturday night, and Austin picked up his phone thinking it was about the science homework. It was, at first. Louis-Felix had sent a photo of his worksheet on arid climates, with a doodle of a camel wearing sunglasses in the margin. Then Marlowe typed, "random question but does anyone know how to read Tagalog," and everything about the conversation changed.

"I can't stop thinking about it," Marlowe sent, in a burst of three messages. "At my grandma's birthday last weekend she gave me a card she wrote herself, all in Tagalog, and I just stood there holding it. I chat with her every Sunday on the phone, no problem. But the card? Nothing. I had to pretend to laugh and say thank you. I felt so fake." There was a pause, then, "Is that weird? Is something wrong with me?"

Austin read the messages twice. Something about it snagged in his brain. Marlowe could talk to her grandmother easily, but couldn't read one sentence from her. That meant the speaking and the reading weren't the same thing somehow, like being able to hum a song but not read sheet music. He typed slowly, testing the idea out loud. "Wait. You speak it at home, right? Like that's the language your family uses. But school and everything outside is English. So you've had years of practice speaking and basically zero practice reading." He added, "I bet if you heard the card out loud you'd understand every word."

"Heritage language," Louis-Felix replied almost instantly. "That's what my cousin calls ours. Haitian Creole at home, English everywhere else. I'm the exact same, by the way. I can argue with my dad in Creole for an hour but I couldn't read a cereal box in it." Austin wanted to verify the pattern before he trusted it, so he asked Marlowe to try an experiment: have her mom read the card aloud, and see how much she understood. Fifteen minutes later Marlowe sent a voice memo. She was laughing before she even got the words out. "It's a joke about me being skinny. I understood all of it. Every single word."

"Okay but the card still matters," Austin typed. "She wrote it by hand. There has to be a way." Marlowe answered with a thinking emoji, then, "What if I learn to read just that one card? Like, actually sound it out, line by line. And then read it back to her on video next Sunday." Louis-Felix wrote, "I'll help you practice. I kind of want to try this with a Creole book my aunt gave me." Austin leaned back against his pillows, phone glowing in the dark, and watched the typing bubble appear under Marlowe's name.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: A desert is often defined as a place that gets less than about 250 millimeters, or 10 inches, of rain a year.
story:
The departures board flickered, and DELAYED appeared next to Eleanor's flight in sinister red letters. She slid down against a pillar near Gate 14, opened her notebook, and stared at the two graphs she had printed before leaving home: monthly rainfall and temperature for the Sonoran Desert and for the Amazon rainforest near Manaus, Brazil.

"Still due Monday?" Genesis asked, dropping onto the tile beside her with her backpack. Across the aisle, Maddie was already three bites into a pretzel.

"Due Monday," Eleanor said. "Ms. Perera said the graphs have to tell the story. Hot season, wet season, all of it. I just can't figure out the rule part. What actually makes a desert a desert?"

Genesis leaned over the printouts. The desert graph was nearly flat, a thin line crawling along the bottom. The rainforest graph climbed in spiky green towers, month after month.

"Look at the scale," Eleanor said. She tapped the desert's y-axis. "Even the wettest month here barely rises. It's like the whole year dwindles down to almost nothing." She traced the rainfall totals in the margin where she had copied them. "Maybe three hundred millimeters total? Less?"

Maddie leaned over, pretzel in hand. "My uncle lives in Phoenix. He says a real desert gets less than about 250 millimeters of rain a year. Ten inches, he says, is the cutoff."

Eleanor wrote it down. "So if a place gets less than about 250 millimeters, or 10 inches, a year, it's a desert. That's the rule." She checked her totals again. Her desert graph came in under the line. The rainforest, near Manaus, towered over it by meters.

"It can't just be heat, then," Genesis said slowly. "Rain is the thing. So what about a cold place?"

Eleanor felt something click. "A cold place could still count, if the rain is low enough." She flipped to the back of her notebook, found the climate data appendix, and ran her finger down the columns until she reached Antarctica. Annual precipitation: well under 250 millimeters. She sat back against the pillar, stunned.

"It's a desert," she said. "Snow and all. A frozen desert." She wrote the sentence at the top of her page and underlined it twice.

"That's your twist," Maddie said, crumbs falling. "Put it in your conclusion."

Eleanor was still writing when Ms. Perera appeared beside their pillar with a cart of coffee. "Storm over the rainforest route," she said, nodding at the board. "We'll be here a while. Show me what you have."

Eleanor held up the two graphs side by side, the flat line and the green towers. "One of these places gets flooded by rain," she said, "and the other gets almost none. And the weirdest one isn't even on my page. It's white and freezing and it still counts."

"Then put it on your page," said Ms. Perera, and walked on toward the window, where the rain hammered the tarmac and the ground crew's orange jackets moved under the lights.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Museums control temperature and humidity because changes make wood, paper and canvas swell and shrink, which can crack or warp old objects.
story:
The bus smelled like sunscreen and paper bags, and Grayson sat with his sketchbook on his knees, drawing the museum's stone front steps before they had even gone inside. He wanted one perfect drawing to enter in the city art contest, and the museum had a carved wooden door from 1802 that he had read about online. When Ms. Crowchild counted heads at the entrance and waved them through, Grayson drifted straight toward it, Parker trailing behind.

The door stood in a glass case, dark oak, with a small metal box mounted in the corner. A needle on the box pointed at a number, and it did not move. "What's that, a thermometer?" Parker asked.

"It's a humidity gauge," said a museum guide who was unlocking a nearby case. "We watch them all day." She moved on, and that was all she said.

Grayson sketched the gauge, then the door, then stopped. He noticed a second gauge in the next case, holding a paper letter, and a third beside a painting on canvas. Everywhere there was wood, paper or canvas, there was a gauge. That was a pattern, and patterns meant a rule he didn't know yet.

He tested it. He walked past cases of stone arrowheads and glass bottles. No gauges. No wood, no paper, no canvas, and no gauges. He came back and stood in front of the letter, thinking about his own bedroom, where his wooden desk drawer stuck every summer and slid loose every winter. Wood swelling. Wood shrinking. If old wood and paper and canvas swelled and shrank the same way, they would crack. They would warp. That had to be why the museum kept the temperature and the humidity steady, so nothing changed size at all. It seemed inevitable that a hundred-year-old door would split otherwise.

"So the gauges are guards," Paula said when he told her. "Invisible guards."

At the gift shop, Grayson spent his money on a postcard of the door instead of the contest paper he'd meant to buy, because the cashier said the shop's revenue kept the special cases running. His mom had promised to buy him proper paper after her shift, and anyway he wanted to try drawing it first on the back of his sketchbook page, just to see.

On the bus home, Ms. Crowchild leaned over his seat. "The caretaker who installed those gauges retired last year, you know," she said. "The new one checks them twice a day. Some jobs never stop."

Grayson looked down at his half-finished door, the gauge drawn carefully in the corner, needle pointing at its steady number. "Then I'll draw the needle right there," he said. "Just where it always is."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: The PG-13 movie rating was introduced in the United States on July 1, 1984, as a step between PG and R.
story:
Piper got to the fountain in Riverside Park ten minutes early, which was a mistake, because ten minutes gave her time to notice everything that could go wrong. The picnic table she'd chosen had a wasp on it. Her hair, which she had pinned up carefully, was already slipping. And the whole reason for this afternoon, a two o'clock movie at the Grand Theater, depended on a plan Kody had described last night in one short text: no parents, just us.

He arrived on his bike, skidding to a stop on the gravel. "Okay, so, change of plan," he said, and Piper felt her stomach drop. "There's an older movie playing at the Riverbend, the one about the emperor of Mars. It's only rated PG. We should go there instead."

"But we've been talking about Night Siege for two weeks," Piper said. "You picked it."

"Yeah, well." He shrugged and started walking toward the duck pond so she couldn't quite see his face. "Night Siege is PG-13. The Riverbend's closer anyway."

Piper followed him past the community garden, where somebody had turned over the dark, fertile soil and planted rows of seedlings in straight lines. That was the moment she isolated the real question, because it wasn't about closeness at all. The Riverbend was actually farther from both their houses. Something about Night Siege itself was the problem.

"PG-13 means parents strongly cautioned," Kody said, before she could ask. "But it's not like R. They can't actually stop you."

Piper sat down on the low stone wall by the pond and pulled out her phone. If ratings had rules behind them, the rules would be written somewhere. She searched, and there it was. "It's not just a suggestion," she said slowly, reading. "The PG-13 rating was introduced in the United States on July 1, 1984, as a step between PG and R. Before that, movies jumped straight from PG to R."

"So?"

"So it's a real category, with real teeth. And the Grand Theater is strict. Remember in March, when they turned away that whole group from St. Brendan's?"

Kody threw a pebble into the pond and watched the ripples instead of answering her. The ducks paddled away from him. Piper watched him too, and the pattern finally assembled itself, the way the seedling rows did: the changed plan, the movie he'd been excited about and suddenly wasn't, the way he'd steered them toward the pond so she couldn't study his face.

"Kody. When's your birthday?"

"August ninth," he muttered.

Two weeks away. He was still twelve.

"You could have just told me," Piper said. She didn't raise her voice, but she didn't soften it either. "I would have figured something out."

"There's nothing to figure out. It's embarrassing."

She stood up and brushed the gravel off her jeans. "The emperor of Mars movie is supposed to be good, actually. Charli saw it twice. But you're buying the popcorn, and you're telling me next time something's wrong instead of making me guess."

Kody looked up, and the corner of his mouth twitched. "Deal," he said, and held out his hand to shake, like they were closing a business deal instead of starting a first date.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Portable generators and charcoal grills give off carbon monoxide, so safety agencies say to run them only outdoors, far from doors and windows, never in a house or garage.
story:
The lights at Grandma's farmhouse went out at dusk, right in the middle of a board game, and Willow's little cousin shrieked like it was the best thing that had ever happened. "Storm's here!" Kruz shouted from the window, where he'd been watching the maples whip around. Chaya lit two candles and set them on the table like tiny trophies, and for a minute it all felt like an adventure, shadows dancing on the old photographs that depicted Grandma's whole life, her wedding, the farm in its early years, her brothers in stiff collars.

Then Grandpa went out to the garage, and Willow heard the rattle of the portable generator being wheeled toward the door that connected to the kitchen. Something snagged in her memory. A safety poster at school, half-ignored at the time, had shown a grill and a generator with a big red X, and a line underneath: run them only outdoors, far from doors and windows, never in a house or a garage. She had thought it was boring that day. Now her stomach dropped.

"Grandpa, wait!" She ran to the garage before he could pull the starter cord. "You can't run it in here."

He looked up, surprised. "Been doing it this way for years, sweetheart. Keeps the cords short."

"But it gives off carbon monoxide," Willow said, the words tumbling out. "Generators and charcoal grills both do. That's why you have to run them only outdoors, far from doors and windows. Never in a house or a garage. Never." Her voice shook a little, but she held his gaze.

Grandpa rubbed his jaw. "Can't see it, can't smell it."

"Exactly why it's scary," Chaya called from the doorway. "You're not immune just because it's never hurt you before, Grandpa Frank. That's like saying you've never crashed so seatbelts are pointless."

"Or like assuming all farmers are stubborn," Kruz added with a grin. "Total stereotype. Some farmers move generators."

Grandpa laughed despite himself, and Willow grabbed one handle of the generator while he took the other. Together they wrestled it out the big door and down the gravel path to the far edge of the yard, well away from every window. Grandpa yanked the cord, the machine coughed to life, and warm yellow light bloomed in the kitchen windows. Kruz whooped. The little cousin cheered from the porch.

"Best blackout ever," Chaya said, and held out her hand for the next round of the board game, played by candlelight anyway.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: No number of white swans can prove that all swans are white, but seeing a single black swan proves that claim false.
story:
Theo's poster had a problem, and the problem was Nour. His hypothesis, printed in blue marker across the top, said that all marbles from the antique jar in his grandmother's attic were glass. He had tested forty-two of them, laid out in rows on the fair table, and every single one was cool, heavy glass. Then Nour walked by, picked up a dull grey marble from the reject box, and scraped it against the table edge.

"Ow," Nour said, holding up his thumb. "That one's not glass."

Theo took the marble. It was heavy for its size and left a grey streak on a piece of paper he kept for notes. "It's a clay marble," he said. "My grandmother said the jar was older than the house."

"So your hypothesis is wrong," Nour said. "Forty-two out of forty-three isn't bad."

"It's not about bad," Theo said. "That's the whole thing Ms. Mansour keeps saying, a hypothesis is a testable guess, and the test is what counts. I couldn't ever prove all of them were glass by checking more marbles. Even if I checked a thousand. But this one clay marble proves the 'all glass' part false." He tapped the grey streak. "One counterexample does it."

Kaydence, at the next table with a sophisticated setup of sensors and a laptop, leaned over. "What happens if you drop your hypothesis and say most are glass?"

"Then I can't be overturned by one marble," Theo said. "But I still can't prove 'most' true, only support it. Forty-two is support." He wrote on a card and clipped it to the poster: forty-two glass, one clay, hypothesis rejected.

Nour frowned at the rows. "How do you interpret the ones you haven't tested?"

Theo turned the jar upside down over a tray. Marbles rolled out, forty-one more, and he began sorting them by colour. "I don't, yet. I test them." He picked up a green one, held it to the light, and felt its weight in his palm. Glass, almost certainly, but he set it in the to-test pile anyway.

Ms. Mansour came by with her clipboard and read the card. "Rejected your own hypothesis before the judges arrived. Good." She made a mark and moved on.

Nour grabbed the grey marble. "I want to see if it's the only clay one. Can I check the brown ones?"

"Sort them by weight first," Theo said, and slid the tray across the table toward him.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Line dances, in which a group repeats the same set of steps facing the same direction, let people dance together without needing a partner.
story:
Lauren stood in her living room with the furniture pushed against the walls, facing the TV. She had watched the video four times, and now she paused it and tried the steps alone. Grapevine left, stomp, grapevine right, clap. Her socks slid on the hardwood, and she knocked her shin on the coffee table, which her dad had missed when he was shoving things aside.

"You're doing it again," said Dylan from the couch, where he sat folding paper airplanes he had no intention of flying. "You keep starting with the left foot. The video lady starts right."

Lauren rewound the clip and watched the instructor's boots. He was right. "Okay," she said. "New hypothesis. If I practice starting on the right foot, I won't spin the wrong way at the dance." She tried it, and for the first time the whole sequence held together, the stomps landing on the beats.

Siena arrived at the door with a garment bag and a bag of chips. "Why is your dad's recliner in the kitchen?" she asked, and then she saw the TV. "Oh, you're learning the Electric Slide. My cousin taught me at a wedding. It's a line dance, so everybody does the same steps, all facing the same direction."

"That's the whole reason I picked it," Lauren said, wiping her forehead with her sleeve. "I didn't want to stand around waiting for someone to ask me, and I didn't want to drag anybody into a slow song either. With this, you just need the steps."

Dylan set down his airplane. "Wait, you don't need a partner?"

"Nope," Siena said. "That's the point. A whole group can dance together and nobody pairs up."

Dylan looked at the TV, then at his shoes, then at the TV again. "Teach me," he said. "Before I regret it."

They lined up all three facing the screen, and the consequence of practicing on hardwood became obvious at once: Dylan slipped at the first stomp and collided with Siena, who grabbed Lauren's arm, and all three of them went down in a heap. Lauren laughed so hard she had to sit on the floor for a minute.

"Again," she said, once she could breathe. They got up. They went again. By the sixth run-through, the pattern that had seemed intricate on the video felt simple, almost boring, and Dylan was adding a little shoulder move on the clap. Lauren told him it was terrible. He kept doing it.

At the dance on Friday, the gym was decorated with streamers, and the DJ announced a line dance. Lauren grabbed Siena's hand, and they found a spot near the front, where a dozen kids were already forming rows. Dylan appeared beside them, sliding into the line a second before the music started. He did the steps perfectly, all of them, even his terrible shoulder move, which two eighth graders behind him copied by the second chorus.

When the song ended, a boy Lauren had never spoken to tapped her on the shoulder. "Hey," he said. "That was cool. Do you want to dance?"

She blinked. "Um, sure, but I don't really know how to do anything without steps."

He grinned and pointed at the dance floor, where a new song was starting. "It's another line dance. Same thing, everybody facing the same way. Just follow me."

Lauren laughed and got in line. After all that practice so she would never have to wait for someone to ask her, she had been asked anyway.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: Under the Treaty of Versailles, Germany lost about 13 percent of its European territory and all of its overseas colonies.
story:
Logan slapped two photocopies onto the library table so hard that the corners curled. One showed Europe in 1914, the other Europe in 1920, and he had circled Germany on both in red marker.

"Look at this," he said. "Just look at it."

Andie leaned over. "Germany looks... smaller."

"It doesn't just look smaller." Logan traced the outline with his finger. "Under the Treaty of Versailles, Germany lost about 13 percent of its European territory. And all of its overseas colonies. Every single one. Gone." He had read the number three times last night to make sure it stuck.

Odin slid into the seat across from them, balancing a tray from the cafeteria. "Why are you yelling at a map?"

"Because tomorrow I have to explain to Ms. Anderson's whole class how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War. She called it a prestigious assignment, her exact word, and she picked me. Me!" Logan's stomach did a small flip every time he thought about it. "But I don't actually get it yet. I know the facts. I just can't make them connect."

Odin chewed, staring at the two maps. "It's like your brother when he lost his bedroom."

Logan froze. "What?"

"When your parents turned his room into an office and made him sleep in the hallway closet. He was furious for months. He said nobody respected him anymore. He started slamming every door in the house." Odin shrugged. "Small thing to you, huge thing to him."

Logan's marker hovered over the 1920 map. A country losing 13 percent of its land and all of its colonies. Not just land. Pride. A whole nation feeling cut down, and people in that nation remembering it, wanting it back, listening to anyone who promised to fix it. He couldn't see that feeling on the map, but the map was evidence of it, like footprints in snow.

"That's it," he whispered. Then louder: "That's it!"

After dinner, Logan couldn't sit still, so he wrote an email to Andie:

Andie. I had it backwards. I was going to stand up there and recite numbers like a robot. Numbers alone won't convince anyone. Tomorrow I'm going to hold up the maps and let the class see the shrink for themselves, then tell them what a country might feel when it's cut down like that. I was nervous about the whole thing. Now I can't wait. You and Odin have to sit in the front row. Logan.

He pressed send before he could change his mind.

The next morning, Ms. Anderson called his name, and Logan walked to the front with both maps rolled under his arm like a general's battle plans. He had even taped them to the whiteboard, angled so nobody could miss the difference. Twenty-eight faces looked at him. He took a breath.

"In 1914," he said, "Germany was this big." He tapped the first map. "By 1920, it was this big." He tapped the second, and a girl in the second row actually gasped.

"Thirteen percent of its European territory," Logan went on, "and every one of its overseas colonies, all gone under the Treaty of Versailles. Now here's my question for you. What would you feel if that happened to your country?"

The room went quiet. Then Odin raised his hand.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: A cow's stomach has four compartments, and the first, the rumen, holds microbes that help break down tough grass the cow later brings back up and chews again as cud.
story:
Nolan pressed his worksheet against the glass of the digestion exhibit, watching the clock above the turbine display. The science center closed its answer desk at two, and the bus left at two fifteen. Whoever turned in the best scavenger hunt sheet won a behind-the-scenes tour of the animal wing, and Nolan had wanted that tour since September. He was three answers short, and the hardest one was the last question: "Why does a cow chew when it isn't eating?"

"They've got a whole hour," Timothy said, leaning on the rail. "You've been staring at that cow for ten minutes."

"She's chewing," Nolan said. The cow in the glass-walled barn stood doing nothing, jaws rolling around and around, slow as something orbiting a planet. There was no hay in front of her. No trough, nothing. "She hasn't eaten since we got here. So what is she chewing?"

"Maybe she's just weird," said Kaius, who had drifted over from the turbine exhibit with his sheet half finished. "Ms. Kelly said the answer desk takes one sheet per group, and ours is due in twenty minutes. We should just write 'because cows like chewing.'"

Nolan didn't move. He remembered the diagram on the wall by the entrance, the one everyone had rushed past to see the cow. He jogged back to it and found it again: the cow's stomach, drawn in cross-section, and it wasn't one stomach at all. Four compartments, labeled in small print, with the first one circled and marked with a magnifying glass full of tiny shapes. Microbes, the caption said. They live in the first compartment and break down tough grass. His eyes followed the arrows. The cow swallows the grass, then brings it back up and chews it again.

He hurried back to the rail, working it through. The microbes lived in the rumen, that first compartment, and the grass needed to be broken down, so the cow swallowed it and returned it to her mouth. She wasn't eating. She was re-chewing.

"She's chewing grass she already swallowed," Nolan said. He flipped his sheet over and wrote fast. "The first compartment, the rumen, has microbes in it that help break down tough grass, and the cow brings it back up and chews it again. It's called cud."

"Say that again, slower," Kaius said, pencil ready.

Ms. Kelly checked her watch from across the room and held up five fingers. Nolan scribbled the last two answers, then ran the sheet to the desk, sliding it across just as the attendant reached for the closed sign.

"Four compartments, rumen, microbes, cud," the attendant read, and stamped the sheet. "Correct."

Behind him, the cow went on chewing, slow and steady, and Timothy laughed. "Even she thinks you've got time to spare."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Practicing in several shorter sessions spread over days usually builds a skill better than the same total time crammed into one long session.
story:
The trumpet had been Ethan's grandmother's, and it still smelled faintly of her apartment, where she had been the longest tenant on the third floor and where the landlord had never once raised her rent. Every Wednesday after school he carried it to the music classroom, where Ms. Tse ran practice sessions for anyone who wanted extra time. He wanted extra time. He just never took it until it was almost too late.

Wednesday came, and with it the lesson, and with it the same disaster. His fingers fumbled the valve changes in the middle of the song, exactly where they had fumbled last week and the week before. Ms. Tse tapped the measure with her pencil. "Same spot," she said, not unkindly. Miley, who was packing up her flute at the next stand, winced on his behalf.

"I practiced forever last night," Ethan said. Two whole hours, in fact, running the song over and over until his lips buzzed and his mother knocked on the door to ask if everything was all right.

That evening he sat on his bed with the music open on his knees, staring at the tricky measure as if it might confess something. He had drilled it at least forty times last night. Forty times, and today it fell apart anyway. That didn't seem fair. Unless, he thought slowly, the problem wasn't how much he practiced but when. He thought about Himmat, who had a legitimate shot at first chair in the youth orchestra and who never seemed desperate before a lesson. Ethan had seen him in the music classroom on Mondays, playing for maybe fifteen minutes, and again on Tuesdays, like it was nothing.

So Ethan tried an experiment on himself. Monday, twenty minutes. Tuesday, twenty minutes, no more, even though he felt like doing the whole hour. Wednesday morning before school, twenty minutes, his neighbors probably hating the high notes. That was only an hour total, the same as one long cram on Tuesday night, and part of him was sure it would signify nothing.

At the lesson, Miley was already there, raising her eyebrows at him. "You're here early," she said. "Who are you, and what have you done with Ethan?"

"Just watch," he said, and lifted the horn. The tricky measure came, and his fingers moved through it, clean, one-two-three, no fumble. He finished the whole piece without stopping, and when he lowered the trumpet his ears were hot and he was grinning like an idiot. "Same total time as before," he told Miley. "Just cut up into pieces over the days."

"Huh," she said. She looked at her flute case, then back at him, and changed her mind about something right there on the spot. "Cancel my Thursday marathon," she told Ms. Tse. "I'm going home tonight instead. I'll be here Monday." Then, to Ethan, quieter: "Fair warning. I'm still beating you to first chair."

The door swung open and Himmat came in with his violin under his arm, glancing between the two of them as if he'd missed something. "What did I walk in on?"

"Nothing," Miley said, already assembling her flute. "Just a new schedule."

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: Frying whole spices briefly in hot oil or ghee, called tempering or tadka in Indian cooking, releases their flavour into the fat.
story:
Nora counted backwards from the moment the flatbread hit the pan, because that was the only clock she trusted. The market stall where she volunteered on Saturdays had one burner, a bag of basmati, a pot of curry simmering under a lid, and Mr. Robinson's cast iron skillet, and her job today was to have all three things ready for the noon rush at exactly the same time. If the rice finished early it went cold and sticky. If the flatbread finished early it turned stiff as cardboard. She had watched the cook do it last weekend, moving between pots without hurry, but watching was not the same as doing.

She set the timer on her phone for the rice, twenty minutes, and started the curry. The recipe said to heat the ghee first and drop in the cumin seeds, let them crackle for a few seconds, and only then add the onions and tomatoes. That order puzzled her. Her instinct was to dump everything in the pot together and stir, which would be faster, and speed mattered today. She almost did it, but she thought of Marlee's mother's kitchen, where the smell of spices hitting hot fat carried out into the hallway before any dish reached the table. Something about the order had to matter, even though she could not see it working.

Marlee arrived with the flatbread dough, which she had mixed at home, because flour was banned from her school lunch table after an incident Nora did not ask about. "Why does it say fry the seeds first?" Nora asked her. "I want to just stir them in later."

Marlee shook her head. "My mom calls that part the tadka. The spices go into the hot ghee, and that's the whole point of doing it first."

So Nora dropped the cumin into the shimmering fat, counted to five while the seeds snapped and darkened, and then added everything else. The smell that rose up was rounder and deeper than anything she had managed at home, where she had always stirred the spices in at the end out of haste.

The timing she solved like a math problem. The rice was mandatory to start first because it took longest. The curry could simmer on low while she rolled flatbread, and the flatbread, which took only a minute per side, had to govern the final countdown. At 11:58 she lifted the lid off the rice, stirred the curry, and slapped the first round of dough onto the skillet.

Mr. Robinson came back from the parking lot carrying a crate of tomatoes, sniffed the air, and raised his eyebrows. "Tadka?" he said.

Nora grinned and flipped the bread. "Last one coming off now."

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: Toulmin's full model has six parts: claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal.
story:
Tyler spread his index cards across the cafeteria table and counted them again. Three cards, three points, each one holding what he thought was a complete argument for the debate tournament that afternoon: that schools should start later in the morning. He had a claim, some evidence, and a sentence saying why the evidence proved the claim. It felt finished, but something about it nagged at him like a math problem where the answer came out too easy.

Gaelle slid into the seat across from him, spinning her own stack of cards. "Mr. Liu gave me a handout on the Toulmin model," she said. "You want to see it?" Tyler said sure, mostly to be polite, because he was certain his three cards were enough. He had built cases this way for two whole tournaments, and one of the judges had even called his second speech "solid." Solid was good. Solid was working.

Then he read the handout, and his stomach dropped. Toulmin's full model had six parts, not three: claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal. He stared at the list, then at his cards. Three whole parts were missing from every single argument he owned. "I've been showing up to debates with half a case," he said.

"More like half of three cases," Gaelle said, grinning. Lea-Rose leaned over from the next table and pointed at his first card. "Okay, so this says students perform better with more sleep. Where's your qualifier? Like, 'in most cases' or 'generally'?"

"That feels like weakening it," Tyler said.

"Last tournament a judge wrote on my ballot that I overclaimed," Lea-Rose said. "I changed my mind about qualifiers after that. They're not weaknesses, they're honesty."

Tyler grabbed three fresh cards for each argument. On one he wrote a qualifier: "in most districts." On another he articulated his backing, the studies behind his assumption that better-rested students actually learn more. His assumptions had been sitting there invisible the whole time, holding everything up like the bottom floor of a building nobody looks at. That was the hidden part, he realized. The warrant and backing were the machinery you couldn't see when an argument worked, only when it broke.

In round two, the opposing speaker stood up and said the plan would cost districts money for new bus schedules. Tyler flipped to his rebuttal card, the one he'd written during lunch, and knocked on the table as if it were a door. "My opponent is right that it's a temporary cost," he said, "which is exactly what my qualifier covers." The judge wrote something down and underlined it twice. When the round ended, Gaelle mouthed "six parts" from across the room and held up all ten fingers, then folded four down. Tyler held up six fingers back, then picked up his cards and started arranging them for the final round.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Yellowstone became the first national park in the United States on March 1, 1872, when President Ulysses S. Grant signed it into law.
story:
The diner sat at the edge of the highway with a neon sign that buzzed like a trapped fly. Austin slid into the booth across from his dad, who was studying a folded map as if it might change when he wasn't looking. Their trip to Yellowstone would take two more days of driving, and Austin had already read his park brochure four times. His little sister kept asking whether there would be bears, and his dad kept saying probably not, in a voice that suggested he hoped so.

A man in a gray hat and a park uniform came in and sat at the counter, and Austin nearly knocked over his milk trying to see the patch on his sleeve. It said Ranger. His dad noticed and waved the man over, because his dad waved at everyone, including a cow once.

"You folks headed to the park?" the ranger asked.

"Yes, and the kids are driving us crazy with questions," Dad said.

"Then I've got one for you." The ranger leaned on the booth. "Tonight at the campfire talk, I stump whole families with this. Yellowstone was the first national park in the United States. Who made it one, and when?"

His dad guessed Theodore Roosevelt. His sister guessed "the bear guy." Austin stared at his water glass and thought. The brochure in his back pocket had a timeline in it, and he had read it on the drive, mostly to evade his sister's singing. He remembered a date, March 1, 1872, and a name that had felt out of place among all the mountains and geysers. A president. Not Roosevelt. He pulled out the brochure, found the line, and looked up.

"President Ulysses S. Grant," Austin said. "He signed it into law on March 1, 1872."

The ranger grinned so wide his hat nearly tipped. "First family in three weeks to get it."

His sister frowned at the brochure. "I thought presidents just got elected and gave speeches."

"This one made a whole park," Austin said.

"Then he's my favorite," she decided, which was abrupt, since yesterday her favorite had been the man who invented ice cream.

Later that evening, in the motel next door, Austin wrote a postcard to his friend Gunnar. He described the diner, the ranger, and the question, and added that he had won a free Junior Ranger badge before even arriving at the park. He also mentioned the puddle in the parking lot that had turned out to be full of tadpoles, and how he had scooped one wriggling larva into a cup just to watch it, then put it back.

The next morning his dad was folding the map differently, slower, like a man who had changed his mind about something. "I thought Yellowstone was just trees and hot water," he said over eggs. "Turns out it started the whole idea of national parks. Maybe we stay an extra day."

"Two extra days," said his sister, holding up the badge, and the waitress, passing by with a coffee pot, laughed and said she'd never seen anyone win an argument with a hat before.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: Under Robert's Rules, a majority vote means more than half of the votes cast.
story:
Abigail climbed the ladder into Elio's treehouse, which was really more of a fort, and a dilapidated one at that. Two of the boards had gone soft and spongy with rain, and the whole structure leaned to the left like it was trying to eavesdrop on the ground. That was exactly why the Maple Street Nature Club was meeting here instead of in Tala's garage. Abigail had argued at the last meeting that the club should vote to spend its twenty dollars on wood filler and new boards, and today, as president, she was going to run the meeting properly for the first time.

She unrolled the agenda she had written on the back of a homework sheet. It smelled faintly of pencil shavings and the orange juice she had spilled on it at breakfast. Item one was attendance, item two was the treasury report, and item three was the repair vote. Last month's meeting had been a disaster, and she kept replaying it in her mind: seven kids talking at once, Tala trying to report on the bird feeder project while two boys argued about whether raccoons were cute, and the whole thing dissolving before anyone decided anything. Abigail had gone home that night wondering how meetings were supposed to work, and her mom, who sat through council meetings for the corporation she worked for, had handed her a battered copy of Robert's Rules. "You can presume it's boring," her mom had said, "but read the first chapter anyway."

Abigail had read more than the first chapter. She had read about agendas, about taking turns, and about votes, and she had made herself a little notebook of rules she actually understood.

Elio came up the ladder next, shaking sawdust off his sleeves, then Tala, then the others until nine kids sat in a circle on overturned milk crates. Two members, Ana and Ben, had said they were coming but never showed. Abigail took a breath and began.

"Item one, attendance. We have nine of eleven." Item two went quickly, since Tala had the club's money in a sandwich bag, all twenty-one dollars and fifty cents of it. Then item three. Abigail read the motion aloud and asked for discussion, and here the magic of the agenda actually seemed to work. Because she called on people one at a time, hands went up instead of voices. Elio said the fort would collapse by winter if they did nothing. A boy named only as the new kid said twenty dollars wasn't enough for lumber. Tala pointed out that the wood filler alone was eight dollars.

Then they voted. "All in favor of the repair motion," Abigail said. Five hands rose. "Opposed?" Four hands. She stared at the numbers, her stomach tightening. Five to four, out of eleven members, with Ana and Ben absent. Did that even count? She remembered a line from her notebook and flipped to it, running her finger down the page.

"That passed," she said slowly. "Under Robert's Rules, a majority means more than half of the votes cast." She counted again to be sure. Nine votes cast, and five was more than half of nine. The two absent members didn't change that, because they hadn't cast anything.

"Wait, so we spent the money without Ana and Ben?" the new kid asked.

"They can bring it up at the next meeting," Tala said. "It's in the rules, I checked."

Abigail wrote the result in her notebook: Motion carried, five to four, two not voting. She looked around the circle, at everyone who had actually gotten a turn to speak, and wondered what else was hiding in that old blue book. "Item four," she said. "Adjourn. Same time next week, and somebody remind Ana and Ben." Elio hammered a loose board back into place with the heel of his sneaker, and sawdust drifted down through the afternoon light like snow.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors, a process called peer review.
story:
The shelf at the back of the pharmacy held two boxes that both promised to shorten a cold, and Bentley meant to find out which one was lying. His mother had been sick for four days, coughing through the walls of their apartment all night, and he had twelve dollars of his own money folded in his pocket. He picked up the first box because he recognized it. A fitness blogger he followed had sworn by it in a post titled "This Wiped Out My Cold in Two Days." The post had hundreds of likes.

"That one's popular," said a voice beside him. Alexane from his science class stood there in a green pharmacy vest, restocking cough drops. "I restock it like every shift. People grab it because somebody online said it worked."

"It did work," Bentley said. "For him. He wrote a whole thing about it."

Alexane shrugged and pushed her cart toward the register, and Bentley stood there holding the box, unsure. The second box sat lower on the shelf, in plainer packaging, and it cost three dollars more. On its side, in small print, it mentioned a study. He crouched down and read the whole panel, then read the first box again, front and back. Nothing. The popular one had a story about one man. The plain one had numbers, a trial, something called a journal.

Mr. Ferreira appeared from behind the counter with a clipboard, checking expiry dates along the aisle. Bentley decided to test his idea out loud. "If I wanted to know whether a medicine actually works, is it better to read a blog where a guy says it cured him, or an article in a journal?"

"Depends," said Mr. Ferreira, without looking up. "What do you know about how journal articles get published?"

Bentley thought hard. His older cousin had gone on about this at Thanksgiving, and he had half listened. "Before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors," he said slowly, getting it straight in his own head as he said it. "It's called peer review."

"That's the phrase," said Mr. Ferreira. He clipped the clipboard under his arm and finally looked at Bentley. "And a blog post? Who checks that?"

"Nobody," Bentley said. "The blogger just writes whatever happened to him." He looked down at the box in his hand, the popular one, and felt his certainty slide sideways. One man's cold getting better could be almost anything. Maybe his cold was going to end anyway. Maybe he got lucky, like flipping a coin and it landing the way he wanted, totally random, and he called it proof.

He tried to classify what he actually had. A story about one person's experience, versus tested evidence that experts had combed through for mistakes. It was like sorting laundry into two piles, and once he saw it that way, he could not unsee it. He put the popular box back on the shelf and picked up the plain one, turned it over, and traced the line about the study with his thumb.

Alexane drifted back over. "You changed your mind?"

"One guy on the internet isn't evidence," Bentley said. "It's just one guy." He carried the plainer box to the register and set his twelve dollars on the counter, three short, then remembered the crumpled bill in his other pocket and smoothed it flat.

"Good choice," said Mr. Ferreira, ringing it up. "Tell your mother to drink fluids, too."

Bentley nodded and pushed through the door into the cold air, the box tucked under his arm like something he had won.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In their 1999 dual process model, researchers Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life.
story:
The car smelled like Grandma's coat, which was folded on the seat beside Mila even though nobody was cold. Her dad was driving them across town to Grandma's apartment building, where the landlord had already taped a note to the door about clearing out the unit by the end of the month. Mila watched the guardrails go by and tried to figure something out, because figuring things out was better than just sitting there.

The thing she was figuring was this: yesterday, one week after the funeral, she had laughed. A whole real laugh, at a video Ellen had sent of a cat falling off a counter. Then the laugh had snapped back like an elastic band, and she'd felt so guilty she'd deleted the video. Today she had cried at breakfast over a spoon, because Grandma had always stolen the good spoon at Sunday dinners. Laugh, cry, laugh, cry. It made no sense, and she wanted to know if there was a rule to it.

"Mom," she said, because Mom was riding in the back with her, Grandma's coat between them. "Did you laugh this week?"

Mom looked out the window for a second. "I laughed at your dad's terrible parking job on Tuesday," she said. "Then I cried in the parking lot. Researchers actually wrote about this, you know. Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut. In 1999 they described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life. They called it a dual process model." She said it flat, like she was reading a grocery list, and then she stared at her hands.

Mila tried the idea out the way she'd test anything. All morning she counted. In the car she thought about the funeral, and it hurt. Then Dad missed the turn and swore at the GPS, and she smiled, and it didn't hurt for almost a minute. Then they pulled up in front of the building where the landlord was waiting, and the hurt came back. Back and forth. Loss, then daily life, then loss again. It wasn't a betrayal of Grandma, the laughing. It was the actual shape of the thing, the way waves have a pattern you can only see if you watch long enough.

Inside the apartment everything was still Grandma's, including the spoon. Mila put it in her pocket without asking, because she was prepared to advocate for that spoon against anyone, even the landlord with his cardboard boxes. Then her phone buzzed. Hope had sent the cat video again, with the message, you deleted it, watch it this time. Mila stood in the little kitchen, watched the cat slide off the counter, and laughed until she had to sit down on Grandma's step stool. Mom didn't say anything. She just sat down too, and put the coat across both their laps.

"Take your time," Dad called from the hallway. "The spoon's not going anywhere."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Astigmatism happens when the cornea or lens is slightly egg-shaped, curving more in one direction than the other, which blurs vision at any distance.
story:
The day Hazel got her glasses, she sat in the back seat of the family car holding the case like it might hatch. The optometrist had slid the new lenses into place an hour ago, and now every street sign they passed stood out crisp and rude, as if it had been shouting at her for years and she had only just turned around. Her mom pulled away from the curb. "So? Better?"

"So much better." Hazel turned the paper bag from the clinic over in her lap. Inside was the printout of her prescription, and above it a little diagram the optometrist had drawn, a circle and an oval side by side. She'd been too stunned in the chair to ask real questions, so she read the sheet now, lips moving. One word stood out: astigmatism.

Her phone buzzed against her knee. It was a message from Lyric, sent in her usual wall of texts: "Hazel. HELLO. Poster due TOMORROW. Saige says ours looks like a smear. I told her that's your artistic style. Please tell me you can still letter the title. We present first period." Hazel typed back with one thumb while her mom merged onto the bridge road. "Getting glasses today. Everything looked smeared near AND far, not just far. That's why the poster looked bad. Not my style." She hit send, then frowned at what she'd written. That detail had bugged her all week. Saige only squinted at the whiteboard, but Hazel had smeared the close stuff too, which was why her handwriting slid sideways and her book spines had to be held at arm's length to read the titles. She'd blamed the lighting, the paper, the synthetic poster board that never took marker properly, everything but her own eyes.

The phone buzzed again. "That's a thing?? Both at once??" Hazel looked out the window, thinking. Near blur and far blur together. That would mean the problem wasn't distance at all, it was the eye itself, doing the same wrong thing at every range. She remembered the optometrist tapping the oval on the diagram. "Your cornea," he had said, "it's called astigmatism. Slightly egg-shaped, curving more in one direction than the other." That was the whole thing. Not weak eyes. Just an egg where a ball should be, smudging light before distance even got a vote.

She typed fast: "New plan. I can SEE now. Drop the poster at my house by 7 and I'll redo the title block tonight. It won't thwart us. Also tell Saige I'm sorry I called her poster border crooked. It probably was actually crooked, but so was I." The reply came back as a row of party emojis and one word from Saige: "7:00." Hazel slid the glasses down her nose, looked at the fuzzy world without them, then pushed them back up and watched it snap clean.

When Lyric's mom's car pulled into the driveway at ten to seven, Hazel was already waiting on the porch with the marker uncapped.

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: In Excel, the PivotTable Fields pane has four areas, Filters, Columns, Rows and Values, and dragging a field into an area decides where it appears in the table.
story:
Alexis sat cross-legged on the living room carpet with her laptop open on the coffee table, glaring at a spreadsheet full of survey answers. Two hundred students had answered the question "Which school lunch do you actually like?" and her job, as part of Ms. Thompson's data project, was to summarize the answers by grade. Sixth graders, seventh graders, eighth graders, all mixed together in one giant messy list. She had tried sorting, then counting by hand, then giving up and eating half a bag of pretzels.

Her friend Dalton sprawled on the couch, tossing a pillow up and catching it. "You've typed the same number three times," he said. "I counted."

"I keep losing my place." Alexis scrolled through the rows. "There has to be a faster way. Ms. Thompson said something about a pivot table on Friday, but I was half asleep."

She clicked the Insert tab and found PivotTable, then jumped when a tall pane appeared on the right side of the screen. It listed her field names at the top, Grade and Lunch Choice and a few others. Below that were four labeled boxes stacked in the pane: Filters, Columns, Rows and Values.

"What are those?" Dalton asked, leaning over the back of the couch.

"No idea yet. Watch this." She grabbed the word Grade and dragged it into the box labeled Rows. The table beside her suddenly showed Sixth, Seventh, Eighth stacked downward. She gasped. "Okay. Okay, that's a thing."

She presumed the four boxes each controlled a different part of the table, since dragging Grade had sent the grades straight down the left side. So she tested it. She dragged Lunch Choice into Columns, and lunch names appeared across the top. Then she dragged Lunch Choice again into the box called Values, and numbers filled the grid, counting every answer at each crossing point. Sixth graders, it turned out, preferred pizza by a landslide, and eighth graders liked the noodle bowl most, which surprised her because the eighth graders always complained about it in the hallway.

"Wait, do it by percentage," Dalton said. "Some grades have way more kids than others."

She right-clicked the numbers and changed the setting to show percent of total instead of counts. The noodle bowl jumped to first place overall. "That changes everything," she said slowly. "The raw numbers made it look like pizza won, but only because there are more sixth graders." She had nearly reported the wrong winner to the whole class.

Ms. Thompson arrived at the door to drop off a signed permission slip for Alexis's mother, and paused at the sight of the screen. "You built that yourself?"

"Mostly by dragging things around until it made sense," Alexis admitted.

"Good. That's how impartial data work. No favorites, just counts." Ms. Thompson smiled at the grid. "I presumed most of you would need a demonstration first. Monday should be interesting."

After she left, Dalton pointed at the Filters box, still empty. "What does that one do?"

Alexis dragged Lunch Choice into it, and a dropdown appeared at the top of her table. She picked one lunch, and the whole grid shrank to show just that.

"Dalton," she said, "we are going to be so ready for Monday."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: iPhones and Android phones let you choose, app by app, whether an app may use your location always, only while you are using it, or never.
story:
Leah had twenty minutes to find a birthday present for her grandmother before her mom finished at the optometrist, and so far the mall had offered nothing but mugs with cats on them. She was on her second loop past the fountain when she heard her name.

"Leah! Over here." Marcel waved from a bench outside the phone kiosk, holding his phone at arm's length like it had bitten him. "You know about phones, right? You fixed Jayla's charging thing."

"Sorted it, not fixed it," Leah said, but she sat down anyway. "What's wrong?"

Marcel held up his screen. A game called Robo Ranch was open, and a little map glowed in the corner with a blue dot on it. The dot was sitting exactly where they were. "Jayla said this game knows where I am. Like, all the time. Even when I'm not playing it."

"That's the ranch game? The one with the bees?" Leah had played it for a week last spring. You built hives and collected nectar from flowers that grew better in fertile soil, and after a while it was all she thought about. Then her data ran low and she'd deleted it without checking anything.

"Yeah. I got a notification this morning saying my hive did great overnight. My hive did great while I was asleep, at my house." He lowered his voice as a woman with shopping bags squeezed past. "And yesterday Jayla texted me from the food court, and the game asked if I wanted to meet her there. It knew, Leah. It knew I was close."

Leah frowned at the blue dot. "So the game can see where you are."

"Can I stop it? Without deleting it? I've got forty levels and a golden queen bee."

The mall noise roared around them, and Leah assessed the problem the way her science teacher, Ms. Balogun, had taught her to assess anything: figure out what you actually know, then test one small thing. What she knew was that phones let you decide things like this. Last term, in the computer lab, she had helped a classmate open settings and find the screen where every app on the phone was listed, and next to each app there were choices about location. An app could be allowed to use your location always, only while you were using it, or never. Three choices. She remembered because the classmate had gasped at how many apps said always.

"Open settings," she said. Marcel's thumbs moved. "Look for the list of apps. Find Robo Ranch and tap it."

"There's a location thing here," Marcel said slowly. "It says always. There's other options, though. Only while using the app. Or never."

"Which do you want?"

"While using, I guess. The map still works when I play, right?" He tapped it. The screen flickered. The blue dot on the game's map faded out, then reappeared, fainter. "It's gone from the corner."

"Open the game and check." Marcel did. The map still worked inside the game, but when he pressed the home button and switched to his messages, the little map in the corner didn't come back. He locked the phone, unlocked it, opened his messages again. Nothing.

"So overnight," Marcel said, "when I'm asleep, it can't see anything."

"That's the point, yeah." Leah checked the time and stood up. "Listen, I have to find a present. But you should tell Jayla, because she plays that game too."

"She plays everything." Marcel was already texting. "Hey, tell her tomorrow. She'll want to see it done on her own phone."

Leah jogged toward the candle shop two doors down, and there, in the window, sat a honeycomb-shaped beeswax candle. Perfect for a grandmother who kept a garden. She pulled out her phone to text her mom, and paused, and opened her own settings instead, scrolling through her own app list to see how many said always.

Six of them. "Okay," she said to the phone. "You're next."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym, and a name outsiders use for it is an exonym; Germans call their country Deutschland, while English speakers say Germany.
story:
The after-school heritage club was supposed to decorate a display case by Friday, and so far it held one conventional paper flag and a bag of cotton balls nobody wanted. Maeva had claimed the Germany section because her grandmother had grown up there, which sounded impressive until Morgane asked which city and Maeva had to admit she didn't know. What she did have was a cousin, Anna, visiting for the month, who laughed every time the family called her German. "You keep using the English name," Anna had said at dinner, waving her fork. "We call it Deutschland."
