At club on Tuesday, Mr. Cohen suggested they label each country with its name in its own language, and Maeva volunteered before Leonie could finish raising her hand. In the art room, a shelf of poster paper obstructed half the window, so they worked in a stripe of yellow light along the median of the long table, Maeva on one side, Leonie and Morgane dragging their chairs over to the other. Morgane printed DEUTSCHLAND in fat blue letters, and Maeva sat back. That was it. The whole fact, sitting right there on paper.

She tested it on the other sections. "What do people in Japan call Japan?" Leonie looked it up on the battered club laptop. "Nihon," she reported. "So every country has two names? Ours and theirs?" Maeva chewed her pencil. Outsiders' names versus the group's own name. There had to be words for that, because there were words for everything, and she usually found them after Morgane did. "Endonym," Morgane announced from the laptop, ten minutes ahead of her, as usual. "A name a group uses for itself. The outsider one is an exonym." Maeva wrote both words on the back of the poster in small letters, in case Mr. Cohen asked.

He did more than ask. On Thursday he leaned over the display case while Maeva arranged the letters, and a mom waiting outside peered through the glass with her stroller parked beside it. "Deutschland," the mom read slowly. "Where's that?" "Germany," Maeva said. "It's what Germans call it. Endonym. There's a whole other word for what we call it, too." The mom nodded and steered the stroller on, and Maeva decided this counted as a victory, small as it was.

She sent Anna a photo of the finished case that night. The reply came while she was brushing her teeth: a single thumbs-up, then "Finally somebody gets it right." Maeva laughed into the mirror, then typed back, "You owe me a postcard from Deutschland. If that's even where you live."

"Obviously," Anna wrote. "Send cotton balls."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Active listening means giving someone full attention and then showing you heard them, for example by asking a follow-up question about what they said.
story:
Lucas had ironed his shirt twice, and it still looked like he had fought it and lost. The date was in two hours, a walk around the mall with Priya from science class, and every time he imagined it his brain went blank except for the sound of his own voice rambling about basketball stats. He called Deven on video and held up the shirt.

"Wear the blue one," Deven said, chewing something. "Also, you sound like a podcast with one listener. You talked the entire time at lunch yesterday. I said my grandma was in the hospital and you told me a story about a buzzer beater."

Lucas sat down hard on his bed. He replayed the lunch in his head and it was true. Deven had mentioned the hospital twice and Lucas had orbited the whole conversation around himself like a planet with one moon named Lucas. "I didn't even ask which hospital," he said.

"Ms. Kaya talked about it in homeroom last week while you were doodling," Deven said. "Active listening. Giving someone your full attention and then showing you heard them, like asking a follow-up question about what they said. Paul tried it on the cashier at the pizza place and got free garlic knots. True story."

Lucas did not trust the garlic knots part, but the rest he could test. He wrote follow-up questions on an index card like game plays: ask about her drawing, her dog, the song she said she couldn't stop humming. Then he folded the card, because pulling out notes mid-date would be negligent, worse than the shirt, and put it in his pocket for emergencies only.

At the mall, Priya said her little brother had broken his arm skateboarding on the garage ramp. Lucas's mouth started to launch the buzzer beater story, and he stopped it midair. "Which arm?" he asked. "The one he writes with?" She lit up and told him the whole saga of the cast, the marker signatures, the ramp her dad had threatened to dismantle, and Lucas just listened, actually hearing it, asking about the ramp, about the signatures. Forty minutes later they were sharing a pretzel and she was laughing so hard about the ramp that she had to put it down.

When she said, "You actually listen," Lucas felt his index card sitting in his pocket, completely unused, and grinned.

"Yeah," he said. "Tell me more about the dog."

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: A first thesis is often called a working thesis because it can change; if the evidence points somewhere else, a careful writer revises the thesis instead of ignoring the evidence.
story:
Charlotte spread her note cards across the kitchen table and read her thesis out loud one more time: "Our school should boycott plastic water bottles because they are the biggest source of litter in our town." The essay was due first period tomorrow, and she still had to build a three-point outline before drafting a single sentence. Point one: bottles fill the storm drains. Point two: bottles cost the school money to clean up. Point three: bottles harm wildlife.

She opened the town's litter survey that she had printed at the library, planning to underline the part about bottles. The numbers stared back at her. Plastic bags and food wrappers made up most of the litter. Bottles were near the bottom of the list, barely a sliver of the chart. She checked the next page, sure she had misread it. She hadn't.

Joaquin knocked on the back door, holding his own stack of cards. "How's your outline?" he asked, dropping into the chair across from her.

"Broken," Charlotte said. She slid the survey across the table. "My whole argument says bottles are the biggest problem. The town says they're not. If I write the essay anyway, Ms. Cho will take one look at my evidence and know I ignored it."

Joaquin frowned at the chart. "So write it anyway and hope?"

She tapped her pencil against the table, thinking. "No. Wait." She pulled out her language arts notebook and flipped to the page where she had copied the board during their essay lesson. "That's why Ms. Cho called it a working thesis. I remember now." She read her own handwriting. "A first thesis is a working thesis because it can change. If the evidence points somewhere else, you revise the thesis instead of ignoring the evidence."

"So change it," Joaquin said.

She crossed out her old sentence and started again, slower this time. "Our school should boycott plastic bags and wrappers, not bottles, because they are the biggest source of litter in our town." Then she rebuilt her outline, point by point, using the cards that actually matched. It went faster than the first version had, because now every piece of evidence had somewhere to go.

At nine o'clock the doorbell rang. Ms. Cho, her neighbor, stood on the porch with a leash in one hand and her dog tugging at the other. "I saw your light on, Charlotte. Rough draft night?"

"Kind of," Charlotte said. "My first thesis was too aggressive about bottles, and the town survey proved me wrong, so I revised it. Turns out that's the whole point of a working thesis." She held up her new outline, the three points lined up clean down the page.

Ms. Cho smiled at the dog, who was sniffing eagerly at the door frame. "Look at him, all eager, like he wants to be the ambassador for every dog on this street. Finish that draft, you two."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848, starting the California Gold Rush that drew people west in huge numbers.
story:
Riley pulled the last box off the cart and set it on the reading table in the city archive, where the lights hummed and the air smelled like old paper and dust. Mr. Szabó had promised the box held settler diaries, and Riley needed one badly. His history project was due Friday, and so far all he had was a paragraph copied from a website that Abby had said read like a cereal box.

"Careful with that one," Mr. Szabó called from the front desk. "It's the oldest thing in this room. Gloves, please."

Riley snapped on the cotton gloves and lifted the leather cover. The handwriting slanted and faded, and half the ink had gone brown, but a date on the first page read 1849. He turned pages slowly, hunting for anything about why the writer's family had left Ohio. He wanted proof, a real reason in a real person's words.

Nyla slid into the chair across from him, peering over his shoulder. "Find anything?"

"Not yet. He talks about the oxen, the river crossings, his sister complaining. Then here, look." Riley tapped a line and read it out loud. "Every man we meet on the trail speaks of nothing but the gold country, and my father, who came for land, now speaks of it too."

Nyla frowned. "Gold country where?"

"California, I think. Wait." Riley sat back. The diary was from 1849, and everyone on the trail was talking about gold. He remembered something his grandfather had said once, about a lucky find at a sawmill. He raised his hand like he was in class. "Mr. Szabó, does the archive have a newspaper from 1848?"

Mr. Szabó checked a shelf, brought back a fragile broadsheet, and laid it beside the diary without a word. Riley scanned the columns. There it was, a notice: gold had been discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848. He read the date twice to be sure.

"So it's a pattern," Riley said, talking faster now. "The gold was found in January 1848, and this family hit the trail in 1849. Some people came for farmland, like the father planned. But once word of the gold spread, whole crowds of people headed west for money instead." He tested the idea against the diary, flipping forward. Sure enough, a later entry read: "We have passed two hundred wagons this week, and every soul among them speaks of California."

"That's actually a real argument," Nyla said. "You're using his diary to show why people moved, not just saying they did."

"It's kind of controversial, though," Riley said. "Half my sources say people left for free land, and this diary says the gold changed their minds halfway. Both things can be true."

"Write that," Nyla said. "Show the diary line, then the newspaper date."

Riley opened his notebook and copied the exact quote, careful with the spelling. His project wasn't done, and Friday was still coming fast, but for the first time he had something the internet didn't: a man long dead telling him, in slanted brown ink, exactly what changed his mind. Riley slid the diary gently back into its box and carried it to Mr. Szabó's desk with both hands.

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: The word monsoon comes from the Arabic word mawsim, meaning 'season', because a monsoon is a wind that reverses direction with the seasons.
story:
Alicia had volunteered to explain monsoons to her geography class mostly because Idris dared her to, and now the presentation was tomorrow and she still could not make sense of it. So when Ms. Owusu suggested the Saturday hike, Alicia brought her notebook, a compass, and two lengths of blue ribbon, and she made Idris and Aurelie carry the sandwiches.

"The problem," she said, as they climbed past a fallen log dotted with orange fungus, "is that I can't see a monsoon. It's a wind over a whole other part of the world. How am I supposed to explain something I've never watched?" Aurelie pointed out that nobody had ever watched a microbe either, at least not without a microscope, and people still believed in those. "Thanks," Alicia said. "That makes me feel so much better about Monday." But she said it while grinning, and Aurelie patted her shoulder as if to console her, which only worked a little.

At the lookout, Alicia tied a ribbon to a branch and held the compass beside it. The ribbon streamed east. "If I come back in a different season," she said, "and the ribbon goes the other way, that would be a wind that flips. That's the part I keep missing. A monsoon isn't just a big rain. It's a wind that reverses direction with the seasons." Idris frowned at the ribbon as though it might trick him. "Then why call it a monsoon and not a flip-wind?" Alicia checked her notebook, where she had copied a line from the library's dictionary the night before, mostly because it looked trivial at the time and now looked like treasure. "The word comes from the Arabic word mawsim," she read. "It means 'season.'" She looked up. "That's the whole clue. Whoever named it was naming the seasons, not the rain. The rain comes because the wind flips, and the wind flips because the season does."

Aurelie sat down on a flat rock and unwrapped a sandwich. "Fine, but my cousin says nobody in her village in Bangladesh cares about wind direction. They care about rice." Alicia thought about that all the way down the trail, stepping over roots, smelling wet leaves and cold pine. By the stream she stopped. "That's the point, though. Rice needs the rain that the monsoon wind brings in, and the fields need the dry season the reversed wind brings, so the farmer plants by the wind even though he never once looks at a ribbon on a stick." She said it slowly, testing it the way she had tested the ribbon. It held.

Back at the trailhead, Ms. Owusu asked what they had learned. Idris, who had spent the whole week insisting geography was useless, announced that he was going to steal Alicia's ribbon idea for his own presentation on trade winds. "You can't steal it," Alicia said. "It's mine." He was already untying the ribbon from her backpack. "Finders keepers," said Idris, stuffing it in his pocket.

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: A tyre's recommended pressure is printed on its sidewall, often in psi or bar.
story:
Levi sat on the wide stone steps of the bank, his bike flipped upside down beside him like a stranded beetle, while his mom was inside signing papers for the loan that would fix the roof but not much else. The front tyre was flat, and he had only the kit she had bought him last week: two tyre levers, a patch kit, and a small pump.

Cameron slid down next to him, holding a slushie. "You're doing that here?"

"Where else? I'm not pushing this thing two miles home." Levi pried at the tyre edge with a lever, and it snapped back and pinched his thumb. He tried again, wedging the lever under the bead and hooking its end to a spoke the way the diagram on the package showed, then working the second lever around. The tyre finally loosened, and the inner tube came out like a long pale worm. Together they searched the tube in the afternoon light until Cameron spotted the tiny puncture, a pinhole that hissed when Levi squeezed it near his cheek.

Inside the bank, behind the glass, Mr. Rahman, the guard who always waved at Levi on Saturdays, watched them with his arms crossed and a faint smile. Outside, Levi glued on the patch and pressed until his fingers ached, then pushed the tube back in and pumped. The tyre fattened, but when he pressed it with his palm it still felt soft, like a half-deflated ball. He had guessed the pressure by feel, so he kept pumping, and then kept pumping some more, until Cameron said, "Maybe there's a rule for this instead of guessing."

Levi ran his thumb along the bumpy sidewall of the tyre, where the raised letters caught the light. There it was, printed right into the rubber: the recommended pressure, listed in psi and also in bar. "It's printed on the sidewall," Levi said. "Psi or bar, both right here." He had ridden this bike for three years and never once noticed. He let out a long breath of air, checked the gauge on the pump against the number on the tyre, and topped it up until the needle matched. When he pressed his palm now, the tyre was firm and solid.

"Careful," Cameron said, sipping the last of his slushie. "That thing's so pumped up it could propel you into next week."

"Don't be pessimistic," Levi said. "It's at exactly what the sidewall says. That's science, not luck."

"You sound like a documentary. A really smug documentary. The kind narrated by a carnivore." Cameron frowned. "A shark narrator."

Levi laughed so hard he almost dropped the pump, and the sound carried through the glass doors, because Mr. Rahman was waving him inside. Levi leaned the bike against the rail and went in, his hands still dirty with grease. His mom stood at the counter with a stack of papers and a tired face, but when she saw him she held up the pen and said, "Last page. Then we ride home."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Complementary colors sit opposite each other on the color wheel, such as red and green, and mixing two complementary paints produces a dull brown or gray.
story:
Caleb spread his brushes across the kitchen table and propped up the canvas he had been working on for three days. The assignment was due Monday: paint a sunset that felt real. His did not. Every time he tried to brighten the orange sky by adding red, the whole thing turned the color of wet dirt, and he could not figure out why.

"Again?" his mom said, glancing over from the sink. "That's the fourth muddy one."

"Fifth," Caleb said. He scraped the palette clean and squeezed out fresh paint, determined to nurture this attempt into something worth hanging in the hallway at school.

He started over with a clean sky, a bold sweep of orange. Then he mixed a dab of green, planning to darken the little hill at the bottom. The moment the green touched the wet orange near the horizon, the paint sludged into gray-brown, like the sunset had been switched for a counterfeit while he blinked. Caleb set down the brush and stared at the mess.

Micah arrived an hour later, carrying two granola bars and no sympathy. "It looks like a swamp fire," he said.

"Thanks." Caleb turned the canvas toward the window. "Watch this." He painted two stripes of orange on a scrap board, then dragged green through one of them. The stripe went dull and brown instantly, while the untouched stripe stayed bright. He tried blue through orange and got the same ugly sludge. "It's not my brushes. It's the colors. Something about them cancels out."

He pulled out his art folder and found the printed color wheel Ms. Flores had given the class in September. He spun it on the table and traced pairs with his finger. Red sat straight across from green. Blue sat opposite orange. Every pair that made mud sat opposite each other on the wheel. "Complementary colors," he said slowly, reading the label. "They're opposites."

"So don't mix them," Micah said, mouth full of granola.

"But I need the hill green and the sky orange, and they touch." Caleb tapped the board where the two stripes had bled into each other. He thought about the poster of Akram's favorite football team, the one with the bright green jersey that seemed to glow against the red background. The colors had not neutralized each other there, because they had never been mixed. They just sat side by side. He grabbed a fresh board and laid down orange, then let it dry while he and Micah looked up a quick anecdote about a painter who had spent a whole summer fighting the same brown sludge in a field of poppies. The painter's fix had been simple: keep the opposites apart.

When the orange was dry to the touch, Caleb painted the hill in clean green beside it, sharp edge to sharp edge, no blending. The green looked greener and the orange glowed hotter than anything he had mixed all week. He held the board up next to the ruined sunset on his canvas.

"That one," Micah said, pointing at the board. "Do the whole painting like that."

Caleb pulled a fresh canvas from under the table and squeezed orange onto his palette.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Dalmatians became firehouse dogs because they got along well with horses and ran ahead of horse-drawn fire carriages, helping clear the way.
story:
The fire history exhibit occupied the museum's east wing, and Aria's class shuffled past glass cases of helmets and coiled hoses until they reached a painting of a spotted dog hanging beside a restored hand-pumped engine. Mustafa stopped in front of it and frowned. "Why is there a dog in the fire exhibit? Did it belong to somebody important?"

Aria studied the painting. The dog stood on a cobblestone street, and behind it, just visible at the edge of the canvas, were the legs and harness of horses. She thought that was odd. A portrait usually centered its subject, but this one pushed the dog off to the side so the horses had to be included. "Look at what's behind it," she said. "Horses. Fire engines used to be pulled by horses. Maybe the dog had something to do with them." Everett crossed his arms. "That's not a real answer. Dogs don't do jobs with horses. A dog guarding the station, that would be plausible. A dog working with horses, no."

Ms. Baptiste was explaining an old hose coupling to a group across the room, so Aria could not ask her. Instead she walked the length of the exhibit, looking for another dog. She found one in a photograph of a fire company from the previous century: men standing on a wagon, horses in harness, and a spotted dog running at the front, ahead of the horses, positioned near the street. In a second photograph, the same breed, same position. She counted four more images, and in every one the spotted dog was out front. If the dogs were pets, they would be sitting on the wagon or beside the men. Being ahead of the horses meant something else. She remembered how riders on the museum stairs had stepped aside for a delivery cart, everyone moving to clear a path. The dog ran ahead to clear the way.

"Everett, come here," she said, and pointed at the photograph. "The dog runs in front. The streets back then were full of commerce, carts and wagons everywhere. The dog goes first and gets people out of the road so the fire carriage can get through." Everett leaned close to the glass. "And the horses let it run right under their feet?" Aria shrugged. "They got along well with horses. That's why firehouses picked these dogs." Mustafa copied the breed name into his notebook. "Dalmatians," he read aloud. "I'm doing my report on them. I called it first."

"You did not call it," Everett said. "I asked the original question. The question counts." Their argument carried across the room, and Ms. Baptiste raised one finger for quiet. She led them toward the gift shop, and Aria noticed the shop window was lined with spotted dog plush toys, a whole row of them. Mustafa groaned, because the museum had clearly known all along.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Endowing means giving your partner a role or trait through what you say, as in 'Doctor, my arm hurts', which makes them the doctor.
story:
Louis had been at drama camp for exactly two days, and already he had a rule: never volunteer for the improv games. The problem wasn't stage fright. The problem was that his mind went blank the instant Ms. Yamamoto called time, and standing frozen in front of thirty kids felt worse than forgetting his lines in the school play, where at least someone whispered hints from the wings.

Then Ms. Yamamoto put the names in a hat, and the hat had opinions. "Louis and Ally," she read. Ally was the one who had performed an entire silent movie in the cafeteria on a dare, complete with a villain's mustache drawn in eyeliner. Wonderful. Louis climbed the stage stairs like a man approaching a plateau of stacked chairs, high and unstable.

"Your scene takes place on a submarine," Ms. Yamamoto said. "Begin." Ally opened her mouth. Louis's brain, true to form, offered nothing. He stared at the back wall. Three full seconds, which on stage is roughly a year.

"Captain, the sonar's picking up something weird," Ally said. Louis felt something shift. She had called him Captain. Somehow that single word propelled his body into a stance he had never practiced, and his voice came out lower and bossier than his own. "Then dive, Ensign. Whatever it is, we're not sticking around to meet it." The class laughed. Ms. Yamamoto held up a hand. "Notice what Ally just did," she said. "That's endowing. You give your partner a role or trait through what you say, and they become it."

Afterward, on the bleachers, Louis turned the idea over. It wasn't a trick for surviving a scene. It was a lever. Whoever spoke first could hand the other person a whole character, and the other person had to accept it. That was the real pattern, hidden under the game. He wanted to test it, and there was only one test subject worth the trouble: Yosef, who had spent two days narrating his own life in the third person and clearly believed he was the funniest person at camp. Louis had found this insufferable. He now found it useful.

On Wednesday the hat gave him Yosef. "Your scene: a birthday party," Ms. Yamamoto said. Yosef inhaled, ready to launch into one of his monologues, but Louis spoke first, fast and eloquent and shameless. "Grandpa, you're a llama. You've been a llama since the incident in 2019, and I need you to accept that before we cut the cake." Yosef's narrating face collapsed. His shoulders slumped into a hunch, his chin jutted, and he spat with great dignity, "Baa." Not the llama noise, but close enough that the room lost it entirely, and Yosef, llama-like and grudging, clopped over on the hardwood in his sandals.

Backstage afterward, Yosef pointed a hoof hand at him. "You did that on purpose." Louis considered denying it. "Grandpa," he said, "yes, and."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: With interest compounded once a year, the balance after n years equals P x (1 + r) to the power n, where r is the yearly rate as a decimal.
story:
Mathis spread the bank's flyer across the kitchen table and pressed the calculator's power key for the third time. The offer on two hundred dollars of savings ended Friday, and his mother had said she would sign the papers after dinner, which gave him about four hours to figure out which account was actually better.

"You're still on that?" Kenna said from the doorway, sneakers dripping rain on the tiles. "It's just a bank."

"Simple pays five percent on the two hundred every year," Mathis said. "The other one compounds."

Kenna dropped onto a chair. "So?"

"So I don't know what compounding does. The flyer doesn't say." He flipped it over. Blank. He tapped the small print: interest compounded once a year. That was all it gave him.

He remembered sixth grade, Ms. Mercado standing at the board while the class groaned through a unit on percents. "One day you'll need this," she had said, and half the room had laughed, and Mathis had laughed too. Now he pulled out his notes from that class and found a single underlined line he'd copied without understanding: with interest compounded once a year, the balance after n years equals P times (1 plus r) to the power n, where r is the yearly rate as a decimal.

"Read that out loud," Kenna said.

He did. Then he turned the rate, five percent, into 0.05, and typed 200 times 1.05, then the power key, then 5. "Five years," he said. "That's when I graduate." The screen showed 255 dollars and change. He checked simple: five percent of 200 was ten dollars a year, times five years, 250. Only about five dollars apart.

"That's it?" Kenna said. "Five bucks? All this for five bucks?"

"Watch," Mathis said, and changed the exponent to 20 years, because he wanted to see the pattern, whether the gap stayed small forever. The compound account pulled ahead by hundreds. He sat back. "It's slow first. Then it isn't."

Kenna leaned over and typed the same thing with 8 percent, doubling the time. "Try this." The difference ballooned. "Okay," she admitted. "That's not nothing."

They ran numbers until his mother came home carrying groceries. Mathis began to recount both results, holding up the flyer, but she cut him off. "The branch called today. They're discontinuing the simple account. I signed you up for the compounding one at lunch."

Mathis stared at her. "You already signed?"

"Yesterday." She set a bag on the counter. "Why do you think the offer ends Friday?"

He looked down at the calculator, at the 255 still glowing on the screen, and realized every number he'd tested had been on an account he'd never had a chance to lose. Kenna started laughing before he did.

"Spontaneous research," she said, wiping her eyes. "Very thorough."

He cleared the screen, then typed it all again anyway, because in September he planned to tell Ms. Mercado exactly what had happened, and he wanted the median of his three trials right.

"Write it down," his mother said, sliding a notepad toward him. Mathis picked up the pen and printed, 200 x 1.05, then 5, and circled it twice.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: At a bar or bat mitzvah, the young person often also chants the haftarah, a reading from the books of the Prophets.
story:
The cultural festival filled the park with the smell of grilled corn and cardamom, and Hailey walked past it all with her practice folder clamped under her arm. She was supposed to be enjoying the afternoon, but the bat mitzvah was in six weeks, and she had only just gotten the Torah portion to stick in her head. She found her friends at the science booth, where a small wind turbine spun above a basin of bubbling water, its blades turning lazily in the breeze.

"You look lethargic," said Hareem, who was holding a raffle ticket and a skewer of chicken. "Eat something. Also, buy raffle tickets, because I want the telescope and I need moral support."

"I can't eat, I have to practice." Hailey tapped her folder. "My Torah reading. I have to chant it by heart."

Gideon, who was leaning on the booth table, glanced up. "Is that the one from the Prophets?"

Hailey stared at him. "What one from the Prophets?"

"The haftarah," Gideon said. "At a bar or bat mitzvah, you often chant the haftarah too, a reading from the books of the Prophets."

"I don't have that in my folder." Hailey flipped through the pages, and her stomach dropped. Her Torah portion was there, neatly highlighted, and nothing else. She had assumed one reading meant one thing to memorize. Two chants, two melodies, six weeks. Behind her the turbine clicked and whirred, and Hareem offered her a piece of chicken as if it were medicine.

That night Hailey tested a theory. Maybe the reason she had been given only one reading was that Mr. Leung, her tutor, expected her to ask. She had been quiet in lessons because she was embarrassed about stumbling over the Hebrew, so maybe he thought she wanted to go slow. The next morning she biked to his house, which smelled like coffee and lemon polish, and set the folder on his kitchen table.

"I don't have the haftarah," she said. "The Prophets reading. I only found out yesterday."

Mr. Leung raised his eyebrows, then pulled a slim booklet from a drawer and slid it across. "I wondered when you'd ask. We'll start with four lines. You chant those, then we modify the tune slightly for the next section, since the melody shifts."

Four lines. Hailey could do four lines. She stood in his kitchen with the booklet open and chanted the first line, wobbly but recognizable, and when she finished, Mr. Leung said it again with her, both their voices rising together on the last word.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: An anecdote is a story about one person's experience; it cannot show that one thing caused another, because other explanations for what happened have not been ruled out.
story:
Charles needed a science article with tested evidence before the library closed at five, and the printer had already eaten two of his dollars. He spread his project sheet on the table: Does magnet therapy reduce pain? Sources required, at least one study with data.

Ziyad dropped into the chair across from him and slid over his phone. "You can use this instead. My uncle wore a copper bracelet for a month and his back pain went away. It's got like four thousand shares."

Charles read it. A man, a bracelet, a recovery. It was a good story, the kind that spread fast, but the project sheet asked for tested evidence. "It's just one person," he said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "The bracelet might not be what fixed his back."

"What else would it be?"

Charles spun his pencil. "Lots of things. Maybe his back got better on its own. Maybe he started stretching, or the pain comes and goes anyway. His pain went away while he was wearing it, but that doesn't mean the bracelet caused it." He tapped the screen. "A story about one person's experience is called an anecdote. It can't show that one thing caused another, because other explanations haven't been ruled out."

Ziyad frowned at the phone like it had lied to him personally. "So four thousand people shared something that proves nothing?"

"For the project, yeah. Basically."

Ms. Murphy appeared beside them with a cart of returns. She had seen the spread of papers from the desk, and she set down two books without being asked. "Pain studies are in the 600s, but there's a review article on the hold shelf under Charles." She noticed his empty water bottle and refilled it at the fountain before he could thank her. "You've got forty minutes."

They found the article: a trial with a real control group, placebo bracelets against magnetic ones, measured results. Charles read while Ziyad hunted through the reference list for more. In one study, people wearing fake bracelets reported the same improvement as people wearing real ones, which meant something else was doing the work. The article even mentioned that people can inherit a tendency toward certain chronic pains, and that our brains' adaptation to repeated signals can make pain fade over time on its own. It was like the uncle's story running on parallel tracks, one track labeled bracelet, the other labeled everything else, and only one study had found a way to tell the tracks apart.

"Grady is going to claim his grandma's honey cured his cough," Ziyad said, printing the article for Charles with his own dollar when the machine jammed on Charles's card. "I'm going to ask what else might explain it."

"Bring me his answer," Charles said. "I'll put it in my conclusion."

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: Peter and Rosemary Grant began studying the medium ground finches of the small Galápagos island Daphne Major in 1973, measuring the beaks of individual birds year after year.
story:
Every Saturday morning since September, Livia had knelt in the mud at Miller Pond with a notebook, a plastic ruler, and a coffee can of mealworms. Her project was to track the same frogs week after week, and she had learned to tell them apart by the pale scars and spots on their backs. She named them all. Frog Seven had a torn left foot, and Frog Eleven had a stripe like a lightning bolt down her spine.

The problem was Charles-Olivier. He wanted a winning photo for the county nature contest, and he had decided the best shot was Frog Eleven eating a mealworm from Livia's hand. "One picture," he said, crouched beside her with his camera. "She has to stay still for half a second. That's all I need." But Frog Eleven was volatile, and on windy mornings every frog at the pond dove for the mud the moment a shadow crossed the water.

That Saturday the wind was calm, and the frogs were feeding. Frog Seven ate four mealworms and sat stubbornly on the flat rock, while Frog Eleven stayed at the shallow edge, snatching worms with quick strikes. Livia measured them both and wrote the numbers down. She noticed something she had not expected: Frog Eleven's mouth was wider than the others', and she caught worms faster in the shallow water where the worms drifted in slowly.

"You always write stuff down but you never say what it means," Charles-Olivier said, resting his camera on his knee. "Do you even have a theory?" Livia said she had half of one, but she needed to check something first. She walked the whole edge of the pond and counted frogs at each spot, marking where the water was shallow and full of drifting food and where it was deep and empty. The wide-mouthed frogs were all at the shallow edge. The narrow-mouthed ones were out where the food was scarce.

At school on Monday she asked Mr. Iyer if she could look something up, and she found the book he kept on the shelf about the Galápagos. There it was: Peter and Rosemary Grant had begun studying the medium ground finches of the small Galápagos island Daphne Major in 1973, and they had measured the beaks of individual birds year after year. Decades of measuring. Nobody had watched the birds change in a single afternoon; the change showed up only because the Grants kept going back and kept their records.

Livia realized she had been thinking about it backward. She had wanted to see a cause directly, the way Charles-Olivier wanted one clear picture, but some causes could not be seen in a single moment. The pattern was the evidence. She also realized that measuring Frog Eleven's head once a week, in the same way every time, was worth more than any dramatic observation, because a pattern needed many numbers stacked on top of each other.

On Saturday she was back at the pond by eight. Charles-Olivier arrived with his camera and a folded lawn chair, and he set it up where Frog Eleven liked to feed. "I'm not leaving until I get the shot," he said. "I refuse to resign myself to second place again." Livia opened her notebook to a fresh page and wrote the date, the wind speed, and Frog Eleven's head measurement. "Then settle in," she said. "I'll be here for years." Frog Eleven struck a mealworm from her open palm, and the shutter clicked.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: The hottest weeks usually come several weeks after the summer solstice, because land and oceans take time to warm up.
story:
Emile's science grade had begun to deteriorate the week school let out, and Ms. Tanaka had given him one chance to fix it: a five-minute explanation, recorded by the end of summer, of why Earth's tilted axis causes the seasons. He had chosen his grandfather's house for the recording because it was quiet, and because Grandpa kept a shelf of old globes, and because Grandpa never asked embarrassing questions.

He set up the biggest globe on the kitchen table and propped his phone against the sugar bowl. In his notebook he had written the whole script, and the last line was the one he was proudest of: the tilt aims your half of the world straight at the sun in June, so the longest day of the year is the hottest day of the year. It sounded perfect. It sounded like an A.

"Who's your audience?" Grandpa asked, shuffling in with his coffee and his pill bottle, which rattled with the antibiotics he was supposed to finish even though he felt better.

"Ms. Tanaka. And whoever." Emile hit record, spun the globe, and delivered the line. Grandpa sipped his coffee and said nothing, which was worse than arguing.

"Say something," Emile said.

"Check the thermometer book first."

Grandpa kept a fat green notebook by the back door with every day's high temperature written down in his small, crooked handwriting, going back farther than Emile had been alive. Emile fetched it and turned to June. The longest day of the year, the twenty-first, showed a mild 24 degrees. He flipped forward, page by page, expecting the numbers to drop. They climbed instead. Late July read 31, 32, 33. He checked three more years. In every single one, the hottest weeks came several weeks after the longest day.

"That can't be right," Emile said. "The tilt is the whole thing. More sun should mean more heat, same day."

Grandpa only tapped the notebook and went out to the garden, where he was trying, without much hope, to convince a neighbor that the snake in his compost pile was not a venomous one.

Emile sat very still. His script was wrong, and the deadline was in nine days, and Ms. Tanaka hated wrong facts more than she hated no facts. He read the temperatures again, slowly this time. The heat didn't arrive with the sunlight. It lagged behind it, like the kitchen stayed warm after the oven went off. The land and the oceans needed time to warm up; that was all the numbers would tell him, and it was enough. He crossed out his proud last line and wrote a new one.

He recorded the whole thing again that evening on the porch, globe wobbling on his knees, flashlight held steady. He said the tilt gave the long days, and then he held up the green notebook so the camera could see the crooked numbers.

"And here's the part nobody guesses," he said. "The hottest weeks show up several weeks after the longest day, because the land and the oceans take time to warm up."

Behind him, coming up the steps with an empty coffee cup, Grandpa clapped once.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: At the Scripps National Spelling Bee, spellers may ask for a word's definition, part of speech, language of origin, or a sentence using it.
story:
Savannah had made it to the county finals, and this year the bee was being held online, which meant she would be spelling from the kitchen table while her dad's old rowboat sat upside down in the garage like a giant forgotten turtle. She used that boat as a kind of rudder for her practicing: whenever she felt herself drifting into panic, she looked out the window at it, took a breath, and steered back to the word list.

On screen, sixteen spellers waited in little boxes. Micah was in the top row, mouthing "good luck" at her, and Idris was somewhere in the middle, tapping his pencil against his chin. Ms. Kerr, who ran the library bee club, sat off camera as the pronouncer, her voice coming through clearly.

Savannah sailed through "camouflage" and "molecule." Then, in round five, Ms. Kerr said, "Your word is 'cayenne.'"

Savannah's mind went blank in a way that felt total. She knew she had heard it, but the letters had scattered like dropped marbles. Her eyes drifted to the garage, to the boat, and she remembered something she had noticed while watching the national bee on television the year before. The spellers up there were always asking questions before they started, and the judges always answered.

"Can I have the definition?" she asked.

"A moderately hot red pepper," Ms. Kerr said.

"Part of speech?"

"It's a noun."

Savannah turned that over. A pepper. A thing you could picture. "Can I have the language of origin?"

"French," said Ms. Kerr.

French. That meant the "ay" sound was probably spelled with an A and a Y, the way it was in words like "bayou." She could almost see Micah in his box, leaning closer. "Cayenne. C, A, Y, E, N, N, E. Cayenne."

"That is correct."

Later, between rounds, Idris sent her a message through the chat that only said, "how did you know to ask all that," and she typed back, "the nationals. they let you ask for a definition, the part of speech, the language of origin, or a sentence. i never used to." She had learned it by watching, the way you learn a current by watching which way the leaves float.

She won on "persistent" in the ninth round, which her mother said could practically symbolize their whole family, especially the year Grandpa's shop nearly closed. The trophy arrived a week later, small and gold, and Savannah set it on the windowsill facing the garage.

That Saturday, Micah and Idris came over to see it. Idris picked it up, turned it over, and said, "Next year, regionals. You're going to ask for a sentence too, right? Ms. Kerr told me a sentence once gave a kid the whole word."

"Every single time," Savannah said. She carried the trophy out to the old boat, balanced it on the stern, and stepped back to look.
